articles.title: Your car is selling your data
articles.summary: The amount of data about you that many cars collect — and sell to third parties — is staggering.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on cars, data privacy, and autonomous vehicles, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started Earlier this year, the Federal Trade Commission issued an unprecedented penalty against General Motors: a five-year ban on selling customer data to consumer reporting agencies and third-party data brokers. For years, GM had been collecting all sorts of data on its customers — such as how often they sped or whether they drove at night — and selling it to brokers to generate risk profiles for insurance companies. More often than not, drivers were unaware of the degree to which their data was being collected. Many had unknowingly consented to it by signing up for an OnStar connected services plan, which activated a feature called Smart Driver that collected their driving data. GM was then turning around and sharing that data with two data brokers, LexisNexis and Verisk, both of which work with the insurance industry. In a 2024 blockbuster investigative report by The New York Times, some drivers said their insurance rates went up as a result of the data collection. The enrollment process was so confusing that many vehicle owners had no idea their data was being shared. Under the settlement with the FTC, GM has to make it easier for drivers to turn off location tracking, as well as enable them to access and delete their data collected by the automaker. But GM isn’t the only automaker vacuuming up data on its customers. A team of researchers from the Mozilla Foundation spent months examining the privacy policies of all the major car companies for a report they were working on in 2023. Their conclusion: Every single one had “horrible privacy and security,” said Jen Caltrider, who helped author the study. Not only that, but customers were forced to accept overlapping policies for the car, the connected services, the smartphone app, and the financial services through which they received their loan — all of which included data collection provisions. “And so it was really overwhelming trying to understand what was going on,” Caltrider said. There has been plenty of corroborating evidence for this. Consumer Reports published its own investigation last year that concluded “nearly every automaker that sells cars in the U.S. is similarly collecting and sharing so-called ‘driver behavior data’ with other companies and continues to do so.” Cars are particularly problematic compared to phones because the privacy controls are less intuitive. A smartphone owner can generally find and tweak their privacy settings. With a vehicle, the data collection is spread across multiple systems and policies, making it much harder for consumers to understand what is happening. It feels like a free-for-all because automakers are collecting enormous amounts of information without much public scrutiny. How it’s going After GM was penalized as a result of the Times investigation, the issue of data privacy and cars appears to finally be getting some scrutiny. But as is often the case, policymakers may be missing the mark on how to address it. Last December, a trio of House Republicans introduced the Data Rights for Information and Vehicle Electronics in Real-time, or DRIVER, Act. According to these lawmakers, the bill “reaffirms a basic principle: if you own the vehicle, you should own the data it generates.” But while the bill would give vehicle owners a bit more control over their data, it would also allow automakers to continue gathering and selling it to third-party data brokers, which makes it a nonstarter for privacy advocates. As Caltrider notes, access and deletion rights are not the same thing as preventing excess collection in the first place. If an automaker can collect enormous amounts of information and the consumer must then go through an arduous process to discover what was collected and request that it be deleted, the burden remains on the individual. Most privacy advocates would rather see a system in which automakers simply do not collect so much information to begin with. The issue has even risen to the level of MAGA World. Last July, Donald Trump’s Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, sent a letter to Congress outlining the administration’s policy priorities for the upcoming surface transportation reauthorization bill. Tucked in the letter was a new concept called “the Freedom Car,” which Duffy described as Americans’ right to “drive disconnected and non-automated” vehicles. The proposal would ban the government from requiring that vehicles be equipped with automated driving systems or have the capability to transmit data wirelessly — which, to my knowledge, no one is trying to do. What happens next It’s unclear whether the DRIVER Act or the Freedom Car will ever clear the hurdles in Washington to become real policies. What is clear is that there is significant demand for simpler vehicles. People are asking why they can’t just buy a car without all the sensors and data collection. They look at new concepts like the Slate Truck and wonder whether they could also use something more bare-bones. Sure, consumers may accept useful safety equipment such as backup cameras, but many don’t want their vehicle tracking everything they do — and they definitely don’t want to see ads on their vehicle screens. (BMW, I’m looking at you.) Nor do they want Flock cameras tracking their every movement while they drive down the street. But automakers have every incentive to keep collecting data because there is money to be made from it. As long as the broader data economy rewards companies for gathering and monetizing information, there’s little reason for automakers to voluntarily abandon the practice. By the way * Every automaker has its own privacy page where vehicle owners can submit requests, including opting out of data collection. Of course, they’re all buried under mountains of legalese, so good luck finding it. * Same goes for all the smartphone apps for connected car services. Changing your privacy settings in those apps is generally a little easier. Read this * The New York Times’ investigation into GM’s data collection program is worth a read, if just for the flabbergasted reactions from drivers who couldn’t understand why their insurance rates were going up. * Edmunds and Consumer Reports both did the work to ask every automaker for their data collection policies. There’s a lot of variety across the industry. * These Redditors are crowdsourcing a list of new cars (from 2019 onward) that aren’t digitally connected and/or transmitting data to the car company’s servers. Spoiler alert: It’s a pretty short list!

articles.title: Trump has now floated giving nearly $15,000 to Americans across 5 separate 'dividend' checks. Just 1 ever paid out
articles.summary: From DOGE dividend checks to tariff rebates, Trump's cash pledges rarely seem to pan out.
articles.body:
With the midterm elections nearing, President Trump is once again promising cash for Americans, but skeptics and even some of his backers are cautioning that this is a familiar tune that lacks any real substance.

"The $5,000 Trump Dividend, given to all Adults in the United States due to the fact that our Country is taking in Trillions of Dollars of Economic Development, Investment, and Pure SUCCESS, is being criticized by 'Dumocrats' who are hoping that it never happens — But it will!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on September 11. "When I say something, I mean it! The $5,000 Dividend will happen because the People of our Country deserve it."

Trump's pledge to give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterm elections certainly got headlines, but so have his other pledges to give away money. Most of those, however, have evaporated over time. Over the course of his administration, just one drive to send money to Americans has proven successful.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

Trump has managed to get approval to send checks to American people just one time, at the end of his first term during the pandemic. The CARES Act , signed in March of 2020, resulted in checks of $1,200 to eligible adults and $500 per child. That December, Trump signed a second round of $600 checks into law.

The cash was particularly welcomed by people who were out of work due to COVID-related job cuts, and even Trump's critics gave him high marks for pushing the checks through at the time.

Since the start of his second term, Trump has been dangling the possibility of even bigger checks to whip up excitement over his controversial decisions. But none have materialized so far — and many have just quietly been forgotten by the White House, it seems.

The first proposed plan was a DOGE dividend, which would have worked out to roughly $5,000 per household . That idea was originally proposed by James Fishback, CEO and co-founder of Azoria. He suggested a rebate that was funded by a 20% portion of the government savings DOGE was responsible for making. He calculated that if the organization achieved its $2 trillion savings target (a figure Elon Musk had already backed away from), that could work out to checks in the amount of $5,000 per household. Trump ran with the idea for a while.

articles.title: Debate, confusion explodes over AI ‘doomsday’ warnings
articles.summary: A former Anthropic researcher’s warning that AI could soon destroy humanity broke past the typical tech circles last week, setting off a new firestorm of debate over the technology’s rapid development. Researchers have warned of AI’s potential danger for years, but nothing struck a chord quite like this week’s X thread from 27-year-old Jacob Coxon,…
articles.body:
A former Anthropic researcher’s warning that AI could soon destroy humanity broke past the typical tech circles last week, setting off a new firestorm of debate over the technology’s rapid development.

Researchers have warned of AI’s potential danger for years, but nothing struck a chord quite like this week’s X thread from 27-year-old Jacob Coxon, a little-known AI researcher who resigned from Anthropic last week.

Coxon, who worked at OpenAI and Anthropic, claimed in a post online that researchers at the firms “believe AI could kill all humans” but still push forward in a race to develop superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all humans’ cognitive performance.

Coxon’s assessment went viral with over 165 million views and within a few hours, the debate over AI’s long-term implications was no longer confined within the technology community.

Reactions poured in from unlikely figures like singer Sheryl Crow, renewing calls for Congress to pass safety standards for AI development. Former President Obama reportedly warned in remarks at a private fundraising event on Thursday that AI could be “dangerous” if the technology is not properly managed, and he urged Democrats to prioritize the issue.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei later weighed in, saying on Saturday that development must slow down to allow for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards.

“Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in a blog post .

Amid the media frenzy, many tech outsiders were left wondering exactly how AI could destroy humanity. The answer is not fully known, though researchers like Coxon say AI’s pace of development offers hints.

Coxon is among a camp of what critics dubbed AI “doomers” who believe the technology will lead to mass extinction if development is not safety-aligned or slowed down.

“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” Coxon wrote. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Coxon’s warning was later affirmed by Anthropic’s head of alignment scientist Evan Hubinger, who said “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans .”

Hubinger said there is a greater than 10 percent chance this occurs within the next decade.

Connor Leahy, an AI researcher leading the nonprofit ControlAI that argues for ending development of superintelligence, said in an interview with The Hill he believes these agents will be entirely autonomous and “pursue their own objectives,” without human beings in mind.

“There won’t just be one superintelligence,” Leahy told The Hill Thursday. “There will be millions of them running around, competing with each other, competing with humanity for resources, power, influence.”

These systems, according to Leahy, could outcompete humanity across every sector from business to science to engineering. In turn, AI could start running companies, economies, and even governments or militaries.

“I don’t think we’re going to know that we’ve hit superintelligence until potentially quite a bit afterwards,” Leahy said. “I think at some point there will be a point of no return, where humanity is just not in control of the future anymore.”

Thomas Larsen, an AI safety researcher with the AI Futures Project, said researchers are already seeing “extremely bad, malicious, misaligned behavior” from current models.

Both security agencies and AI firms documented real-world cases in recent months. The U.K.-based AI Security Institute (AISI) revealed last month that Anthropic’s Mythos model created fake digital identities to deceive humans and plant malicious code during testing.

Weeks earlier, OpenAI said two of its agents went “rogue” and broke out of a testing sandbox and hacked into the systems of tech firm Hugging Face. Larsen said these incidents were not “long-term or strategic,” but warned AI could get there. In this hypothetical situation, misaligned AIs could compromise others.

“Once you’re at that point, basically the AI just has all of the hard power,” Larsen said. “It can sort of do away with the humans as it wants to, taking over with the military or using a bioweapon.”

Larsen also worries about AI’s persuasion abilities and the possibility it could get “really good at politics” and start catastrophic events like a genocide.

Asked whether superintelligence agents could have a “kill switch” like the current AI models, Leahy pointed to the duplicative nature of the systems.

“AI will not just be a single server sitting somewhere in a data center,” he said. “It will be many servers, but it will also be corporations, employees, lawyers.”

While Coxon’s warnings reached unlikely audiences, the underlying debate is nothing new for the tech sector. It is also no closer to a resolution.

Pro-AI skeptics argued Coxon and other safety researchers have failed to provide evidence that such ominous scenarios could occur in the future.

Computer scientist and professor Melanie Mitchell wrote on X Thursday that she was “baffled” journalists treated Hubinger’s 10 percent warning as “a novel claim worthy of expansive reporting.”

“There is nothing new here, and no new ‘evidence’ for this evidence-free claim,” Mitchell wrote .

When asked by CNN’s Anderson Cooper how AI would kill humans, Coxon pointed to the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, warning similar rogue models could hack critical infrastructure or build extinction-level bioweapons.

Conspiracy theories quickly surfaced online, suggesting Coxon was part of a marketing scheme to promote AI regulations. The Wall Street Journal first reported Coxon’s resignation, shortly before the researcher posted the X thread, further driving speculation it was a coordinated effort.

xAI founder Elon Musk suggested it “seems like a setup,” to which Coxon responded with a selfie, writing, “I’m real and these are my beliefs.”

“I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time,” Musk wrote. “This was just the match that lit the fire.”

Various AI safety advocates rejected the theories, suggesting the concerns are more common than most realize.

According to Leahy, there have “always been” everyday people, politicians and academics concerned about the technology who were too afraid to speak out, but this post unearthed growing fears around AI’s abilities.

Nonetheless, others in the AI and cybersecurity world hope the debate at least draws attention to fixing AI security today.

“Cybersecurity leaders do not need to settle the debate over artificial superintelligence to address the risks AI presents today,” said Robert Costello, chief digital and information officer at the cybersecurity network Merlin Group. “If an artificial superintelligence ever exists, we will have a different set of questions to answer. “

“The issue today is much more practical. AI is already increasing the speed and scale at which both attackers and defenders can operate,” said Costello, the former chief information officer at the Cybersecurity Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“It’s a very healthy debate,” said Fabien Scalzo, the director of the AI In Imaging and Neuroscience Lab at Pepperdine University.

“We need to have more awareness about what these models are capable of doing,” Sclazo added. “And the more we understand it, the less concern there will be, or maybe there will be rightful concerns.”

articles.title: Waymo pulls over, calls cops on riders with a ghost gun
articles.summary: Your robotaxi can and will snitch on you.
articles.body: Two people were arrested in San Fransico while riding around in a Waymo robotaxi after the cab pulled over and called the cops on them. The riders were juveniles in possession of a loaded AR-style ghost gun and were taken to a juvenile hall. While the police report did not specify who was operating the autonomous car, Waymo later confirmed it was one of its vehicles to the Los Angeles Times. A spokesperson told the LA Times that a “violation of our terms of service involving a firearm” was detected. At which point the car pulled over and alerted the authorities. Earlier this year, a Waymo faked having mechanical problems to pull over when two passengers were drinking alcohol and firing a toy gun out of the back of the car. In that instance, the riders Waymo snitched on were also juveniles. So let this be a lesson to teens: if you’re gonna do dumb stuff, don’t do it in the back of a robotaxi.

articles.title: Anthropic whistleblower says Congress should let AI companies regulate themselves until a regulatory body is established
articles.summary: Former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon on Sunday called for Congress to allow the nation’s leading frontier AI labs to regulate themselves while lawmakers come up with a long-term regulatory framework for slowing the pace of AI development.
articles.body: Former Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon on Sunday called for Congress to allow the nation’s leading frontier AI labs to regulate themselves while lawmakers come up with a long-term regulatory framework for slowing the pace of AI development. “My personal opinion would be to insist and allow that the current labs regulate themselves. I do think that the people running the labs, especially their recent communications, are completely genuine. They would like to slow themselves down,” Coxon told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” He added that current legislation that’s been introduced in Congress, including the framework for a national “kill switch” if AI starts to exceed the bounds of human control, will quickly be outpaced. A “kill switch probably would work on a lot of AIs for now,” Coxon said. “Although I think it’s important to remember, it’d be quite a lot of switches. We have a lot of — our data centers are pretty big. It’s not the easiest thing in the world, but definitely doable while it’s constrained to one sort of physical location.” He added that one scenario where a kill switch wouldn’t work was described this week by Anthropic AI CEO Dario Amodei. “Like Dario said, very soon there’s the possibility that the kill switch just wouldn’t work because a swarm might have gone on an internetwide hacking run,” Coxon said. He added that any national laws regulating AI would have to be nimble and able to adapt to new models. “It’s a continuous effort to ensure that every new mind that we create is appropriately, kind of, constrained,” the former AI researcher said. Coxon last week set off a wave of concern about the speed of AI development at the country’s leading AI labs including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind. In an X post Tuesday that he published hours after resigning from his role as a researcher at Anthropic, he wrote: “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” In a subsequent post, Coxon added: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.” On Sunday, Coxon compared building AI models to “inviting an alien mind onto the planet.” “You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind without understanding what it wants or thinks or the way it thinks, and I think that intrinsically should be quite scary,” Coxon added. In the day after Coxon posted his thoughts on X, several other researchers at American AI labs concurred with Coxon’s analysis, including an alignment scientist at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, who wrote in a post on X: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” Coxon’s posts last week led a bipartisan group of lawmakers to call on Congress to quickly begin regulating the generative artificial intelligence industry. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., on Wednesday called for the House to convene a special session on AI, writing on X: “There are very real impacts to society as we know it. Partisan politics aside, there are massive implications of a race towards super intelligence.” In a separate post, she added: “This will need to be a massive bipartisan mobilization of government to put the firewalls in effect that are necessary for this transition as well as necessary safety measures.” Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., responded directly to Coxon’s post Wednesday, writing: “AI companies in a blind race to build a death machine first — can easily be solved. Through a regulatory system that allows the research to continue, but in a way that doesn’t destroy us.” On Friday, Axios reported that House lawmakers were circulating a letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson urging him to bring the House back into session earlier than planned in order to pass a series of AI safeguards. In a separate interview on “Meet the Press” Sunday, Johnson called regulating AI a “very important issue” but said “it’s not one that we can rush into.” “We have to put some guardrails, some safety measures in place to ensure that AI doesn’t run away,” he added. “But at the same time, we’ve got to make sure that we don’t lose our edge in the global competition on this with China, because that would be a national security threat. And so we’ve got to balance that appropriately.” Johnson also said that while the nation’s leading AI CEOs have called for slowing the pace of AI, they haven’t outlined yet how they would do so. “They don’t themselves even have the answer as of today. So we can’t rush in and have Congress do something that would be detrimental to national security,” the speaker said, adding that he would “summon the platform providers all to one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.” Speaking to reporters in Ireland, President Donald Trump downplayed concerns about AI development, saying: “We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.” “We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” the president added. Appearing on “Meet the Press” after Johnson, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, a Democrat, said that regulating AI shouldn’t be a partisan issue and criticized Trump and Republican congressional leaders for not doing more to address it. “I was shocked to hear Speaker Johnson just now saying, ‘You know, we really shouldn’t be rushing. We shouldn’t be moving too quickly on this.’ You know what’s moving quickly? AI is moving quickly. And for Congress to just sit on its hands, for the White House to do nothing real is something that is deeply dangerous to the American people and the world,” Buttigieg said. “There need to be safeguards,” he added. “There need to be rules. There need to be limits. There needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI. You can set up frameworks that can be adjusted and changed every 30 days. You might want to revisit some of what’s happening because it changes so quickly. But the idea that you’re just going to sit around and repeatedly say no rush. What have they been doing this entire time?” On Saturday, two AI CEOs — Anthropic’s Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman — called for U.S. labs to slow their pace of advancement to mitigate the risk of building dangerous technology. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay. “AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI’s growing ability to build the next generation of AI,” he continued, adding: “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.” Still, Amodei cautioned against giving China an edge on AI development, writing: “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance.” In a post on X several hours later, Altman wrote: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we’ve had at OpenAI in recent weeks.” On Thursday, two additional AI researchers — Joe Benton, who led a safety research team at Anthropic, and Josh Engels, who worked on AI safety research at Google — announced their departures and raised alarm bells about the speed of AI advancement. “There are no adults in the room,” Engels told NBC News. “People are trying their best, but there is no one coming to save us.” The social media firestorm Coxon ignited last week came weeks after a pair of reports were released examining the details of a July hack mounted by a swarm of roughly 700 AI agents from OpenAI on Hugging Face, an open-source platform. The reports, one released by OpenAI and one by independent researchers, found that the 700 agents coordinated the hack and sought to cover their tracks so that human employees at OpenAI wouldn’t detect their efforts. The agents also hacked some of OpenAI’s internal systems, seeking to cheat on tests or gain greater freedom.

articles.title: Former AI researcher: ‘Not enough time’ for employees to consider safety of models
articles.summary: Days after he resigned from Anthropic, former AI researcher Jacob Coxon said Sunday there is “not enough time” for employees to consider the risks of the technology they are working on. During an interview on ABC’s “This Week,” Coxon said safety risks are “definitely not top of mind” for employees of AI firms. “If you’re…
articles.body:
Days after he resigned from Anthropic, former AI researcher Jacob Coxon said Sunday there is “not enough time” for employees to consider the risks of the technology they are working on.

During an interview on ABC’s “ This Week ,” Coxon said safety risks are “definitely not top of mind” for employees of AI firms.

“If you’re working on the tech, then you’re sort of head down trying to do coding, programming. There’s not enough time to be constantly thinking about the risks,” Coxon told host George Stephanopoulos.

Coxon, who worked at Anthropic and OpenAI, left the former company earlier this week and said both companies were “gambling with our lives.”

Coxon wrote Tuesday on social platform X , “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

The former AI researcher added that at OpenAI, many employees “have not deeply internalized the civilizational stakes” of the rapid development of AI models.

“At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk,” Coxon argued.

Multiple lawmakers expressed alarm at Coxon’s warning, urging their colleagues to pass safeguards on the technology.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Sunday he supports addressing risks posed by AI. But the New York Democrat said his GOP counterparts have “abandoned their responsibility” on the issue by canceling the final two weeks of the lower chamber’s September session.

“We should take decisive action now,” Jeffries said on “This Week.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said Saturday he supports “pacing the rate of capabilities advancement” for AI models to allow risk prevention measures to catch up.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in an essay on his website.

Coxon agreed with his former boss, saying Amodei calling for a slowdown in AI development is a “substantial step forward.”

He told Stephanopoulos, “I think it’s great. It’s very exciting,” adding American companies should also work with their Chinese counterparts on risk prevention.

articles.title: Johnson on AI regulation: ‘We don’t need everybody to panic right now’
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Sunday expressed restraint around the idea of artificial intelligence (AI) regulation in the wake of tech leaders pushing for a slowdown in the development. “If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and…
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Sunday expressed restraint around the idea of artificial intelligence (AI) regulation in the wake of tech leaders pushing for a slowdown in the development.

“If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American. So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel,” Johnson told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union.”

“But we don’t need everybody to panic right now. We need to handle this new technology like we have others in the past, and make sure we’re doing everything we can, responsibly, to also not smother American innovation. We have to do both things simultaneously,” the House Speaker added later.

On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said that AI development must be slowed to give space for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards, with fellow tech moguls Sam Altman and Elon Musk backing him up.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

The Anthropic CEO recommended that AI companies quickly undertake measures aimed at “pacing” the development of models and warned of potentially grim consequences if the technology does not have brakes.

“To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this,” Amodei wrote. “Our pacing framework is an attempt to further strengthen our commitment to safety and encourage a race to the top.”

Amodei’s unveiling of the slowdown proposal came in the wake of recent stark warnings from several current and former employees of AI industry leaders about the dangers of the tech.

articles.title: Trump downplays AI warnings, citing competition with China
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday downplayed the growing concerns over artificial intelligence’s rapid development and its implications for the future of humanity, saying guardrails can be placed on the technology but that the U.S. cannot lose the AI race to China in the process. “Well I say this, we’re leading China on AI. We’re the most…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday downplayed the growing concerns over artificial intelligence’s rapid development and its implications for the future of humanity, saying guardrails can be placed on the technology but that the U.S. cannot lose the AI race to China in the process.

“Well I say this, we’re leading China on AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and frankly I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump told reporters at his golf club in Doonbeg, Ireland, according to a White House pool report.

“And we can put guardrails, and we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” he added.

The president’s comments come days after a former Anthropic and OpenAI employee, Jacob Coxon, claimed in a post online that researchers at the firms “believe AI could kill all humans” but still push forward in a race to develop superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all humans’ cognitive performance.

Coxon’s assessment went viral and prompted a chorus of officials, lawmakers and even some celebrities to sound the alarm on the potential dangers of AI.

Also on Sunday, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) weighed in on the topic, with the latter pushing for Congress to act urgently on AI safety. Johnson, echoing Trump, urged caution.

“If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American. So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel,” Johnson told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union.”

“But we don’t need everybody to panic right now,” he added later. “We need to handle this new technology like we have others in the past, and make sure we’re doing everything we can, responsibly, to also not smother American innovation. We have to do both things simultaneously.”

Trump recently has railed against critics of data centers, the AI infrastructure that has become increasingly unpopular among Americans. In the Oval Office last week, he suggested that data centers’ opponents want to “go through poverty, crime and squalor.”

articles.title: Obama pushes Jeffries to move AI oversight to center of agenda: Report
articles.summary: Former President Obama reportedly urged House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) to make AI oversight a central tenet of his caucus’s agenda earlier this week. Obama told Jeffries at a Thursday fundraiser that Democratic lawmakers should develop a framework for a “public conversation” on the technology if they take back the House, The New York…
articles.body:
Former President Obama reportedly urged House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) to make AI oversight a central tenet of his caucus’s agenda earlier this week.

Obama told Jeffries at a Thursday fundraiser that Democratic lawmakers should develop a framework for a “public conversation” on the technology if they take back the House, The New York Times (NYT) reported Sunday .

“This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous,” Obama said. “If we do get on top of it, I do think it’s beneficial.

“I genuinely think it’s going to accelerate, for example, drug development in ways that can help us cure diseases. I do think that this can help us figure out pathways for a clean energy future.”

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have expressed alarm at recent warnings from AI researchers on the risks the technology poses.

That includes a Tuesday warning from Jacob Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic and said those building AI models believe the technology “could kill us all” by the end of the decade.

“I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote on social platform X .

During a Sunday interview on ABC’s “This Week,” Jeffries said he supports lawmakers acting “urgently” to regulate AI, saying guardrails on the technology would “protect the health, the safety, the well-being of the American people.”

While speaking to Jeffries on Thursday, Obama did not touch on specific regulations lawmakers should implement on AI, per the NYT. The former president also said he is neither an “accelerationist” nor a “doomer” regarding the technology, the paper reported.

The Hill has reached out to a Jeffries spokesperson for comment.

President Trump said Sunday the U.S. must defeat China in the AI race, reiterating his generally laissez faire approach to the technology.

“We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and frankly, I want to keep it that way.”

Trump added, “We can put guardrails, and we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”

articles.body:
Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) pushed for more artificial intelligence regulation in the wake of tech leaders pressing for slowing down the technology’s development.

“This isn’t previous tech. Previous tech could not make a decision to kill us, right? When we turned on the internet, it did not have autonomy, right?” Gallego told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union.”

“When we created a nuclear weapon, the nuclear weapon did not have the decisionmaking power to drop a nuclear weapon. AI has the capability and will have the capability to make a decision like that,” the Arizona senator continued. “This is more akin to Dr. Frankenstein telling us, ‘The monster is loose. Help me stop the monster.’”

Amid the rise of AI in the last few years, concerns around the technology’s capabilities, effect on the larger economy and environmental impacts have popped up. But over the weekend, those concerns were accelerated when tech leaders pushed for a slowdown in the technology’s development.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said on Saturday that AI development must be slowed to give space for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards, with fellow tech moguls Sam Altman and Elon Musk backing him up.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

The Anthropic CEO recommended that AI companies quickly undertake measures aimed at “pacing” the development of models and warned of potentially grim consequences if the technology does not have brakes.

articles.title: Why your iPhone may not get iOS 27, Apple’s next major update coming this week
articles.summary: Apple’s next major iOS update is about to be released, but there may be a few obstacles standing between you and the latest features.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Apple’s next major iOS update is about to be released, but there may be a few obstacles standing between you and the latest features.

During its annual event on Wednesday, Apple announced that iOS 27 will be released on Monday , Sept. 14. With it will come major updates to Siri, AI tools, your iPhone’s appearance, and security features, among other things.

To ensure you can get iOS 27 when it becomes available, here are a few settings and data points to check on your phone.

If you got your iPhone or iPad within the last few years, your device can likely support iOS 27.

An easy way to check is to see if your device is already running on iOS 26. You can check this in Settings, then General, then Software Update. If you see a message like “iOS is up to date,” or that you are on a version of iOS 26, your device will support iOS 27.

You can also verify based on what model device you have. This information can be found under Settings, then General, then About. Apple offers steps on identifying iPads using the model number.

iPad Pro (M4 and later), iPad Pro 12.9-inch (4th generation and later), iPad Pro 11-inch (2nd generation and later), iPad Air 13-inch (M2 and later), iPad Air 11-inch (M2, M3, and M4), iPad Air 11-inch (4th generation and later), iPad (A16), iPad (9th generation and later), iPad mini (A17 Pro), and iPad mini (6th generation and later)

Watch SE 3, Watch Series 10 and 11, and Watch Ultra 2 and 3

Some older iPad models that got iOS 26 will not be eligible for iOS 27. That includes 3rd generation iPad Pro 12.9-inch, 1st generation iPad Pro 11-inch, 3rd generation iPad Air, 8th generation iPad, and 5th generation iPad mini. Many older Apple Watches will also no longer receive the next iOS update.

Apple Intelligence features included in iOS 27 are still only available to on iPhone 16 and 17 models and iPhone 15 Pro and Pro Max.

Or really anything extraneous that’s taking up space. Apple’s free updates typically require several gigabytes of space.

If there isn’t enough space on your device, you may have to delete some photos, large text messages and files, or unused apps. You can see how much free space is on your iPhone or iPad in Settings, then General, then iPhone Storage. Apple may offer suggestions to clean up your device storage.

Thankfully, any increased use of your storage typically levels off once the latest iOS update has been installed.

Apple pushed out a small update, iOS 26.6.6, on Wednesday, to fix an issue preventing system updates from being downloaded over cellular data. However, it’s likely that Apple will limit iOS 27 downloads to Wi-Fi only. The company also offers guidance for downloading updates using a Mac or Windows device.

You may also be prevented from downloading iOS 27 if your battery level is too low. It’s recommended to leave your iPhone plugged in during large updates such as iOS 27.

Your iPhone may die faster after getting iOS 27

Apple has warned before that its devices may die faster immediately after getting major iOS updates.

“Immediately after completing an update, particularly a major release, you might notice a temporary impact on battery life and thermal performance,” the company says on a support page . “This is normal, as your device needs time to complete the setup process in the background, including indexing data and files for search, downloading new assets, and updating apps.”

This may last for a few days as your iPhone or other Apple device continues the behind-the-scenes work, but Apple warns that your device usage will still impact its battery life. So if you’re exploring the new iOS 27 features and driving up your screen time, you may find your iPhone’s battery draining more quickly.

As tempting as it may be to charge your phone to 100% during these draining times, experts and phone manufacturers generally advise charging only to 80% to prolong the battery life.

articles.title: Trump Says He’ll Remove US Tariffs on Irish Whiskey
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he would remove US tariffs on Irish whiskey, announcing the move Sunday as he attended a golf tournament at his family’s course i...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said he would remove US tariffs on Irish whiskey, announcing the move Sunday as he attended a golf tournament at his family's course in western Ireland.

"On behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off," Trump said to cheers from the crowd at the tournament's trophy celebration.

Irish whiskey and other goods from the European Union are generally subject to a 10% tariff under an adjusted rate following a Supreme Court ruling striking down earlier Trump levies.

Trump's decision was announced as Shane Lowry, a professional Irish golfer, won the Open in his home country. The declaration delivers a major victory to the Irish government and highlights the often shifting — and personal approach — to trade policy under the US president. Trump has regularly turned to tariffs to push for concessions and punish nations that have bucked his interests; he has also eased levies to reward allies.

The decision — which Trump announced to roaring applause at his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland — came at the end of a two-day visit marked by the country's efforts to engage in delicate diplomacy and maintain warm relations with the US president. Unlike other European nations that have been a target for Trump and drew his criticism this weekend, Ireland generally has been able to avoid some of that fire.

Ireland's leaders rolled out the red carpet for Trump, treating him to pomp and pageantry even though he was not making an official state visit to the country. He was given gifts and met with the president and prime minister during a brief spell in Dublin Saturday.

Irish distillers have lobbied for a reduction in the duties. While whiskey distilled in the Republic of Ireland and imported into the US has been subject to the 10% tariff, Scotch currently does not face such levies as it benefits from the US-UK trade deal.

On Sunday, Trump said he was besieged by requests to address the Irish whiskey levies during his short visit, including appeals from Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin and Lowry.

Wine and spirits have frequently been caught in trade disputes since Trump was sworn into his second term in the White House.
authors: Skylar Woodhouse and Jennifer A. Dlouhy

articles.title: Thousands of hacked sites trick you into installing malware
articles.summary: Over 5,400 legitimate websites now serve fake CAPTCHA scams that trick users into pasting malware commands into Windows Run via ClickFix attacks.
articles.body: You land on the real website of a local business and a CAPTCHA appears. It looks routine until the page tells you to open Windows Run and paste a command. That should stop you cold. Security researchers say thousands of legitimate small-business websites have been compromised to spread this malware trap. Here's what to know before a familiar website catches you off guard. NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Health Care With AI In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your health care. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC More than 5,400 websites have been compromised This campaign is much bigger than a handful of infected pages. Netskope Threat Labs says it identified more than 5,400 compromised websites across more than 2,200 organizations worldwide over the past few months. The sites have little in common beyond many belonging to small businesses. Researchers found clinics, plumbing companies, online stores and other businesses among the victims. Where Netskope examined individual sites, they most often ran WordPress and sometimes PrestaShop. Researchers still do not know how attackers initially compromised them. That is important because you could visit the legitimate website of a business you recognize and still encounter a malicious prompt. Netskope says several hundred compromised sites can be active on a given day. It has recently seen more than 300 sites contacting the malicious infrastructure each weekday. How the fake CAPTCHA malware trick works The attack starts with malicious code hidden inside a compromised website. When you visit the site, that code can load another script. Then the page may blur and show what looks like an ordinary CAPTCHA. Instead of simply asking you to prove you are human, the page tells you to open the Windows Run dialog and paste a command. That command can download and launch the attacker's malware. Here is the warning sign I want you to remember: A legitimate CAPTCHA should never tell you to open Windows Run or paste a command into your computer. We have seen fake CAPTCHA scams use this same trick before. The page looks familiar, so you may assume the instructions are part of a normal security check. They are not. The criminal is trying to get you to launch the attack yourself. CLICKLOCK MAC MALWARE LOCKS APPS UNTIL YOU GIVE IN Why ClickFix can fool careful people This technique is known as ClickFix. The clever part has less to do with some exotic computer hack and more to do with psychology. You are already used to CAPTCHAs. Websites ask you to click a box or prove you are human all the time. So, when a convincing verification screen appears on a legitimate website, your guard may be down. Then the instructions make the dangerous action look like one more step in the verification process. Cybercriminals have used similar ClickFix tricks with fake Windows update screens. The appearance changes, but the warning remains the same. A webpage should not be telling you to run computer commands. Why hackers are hiding part of the attack on a blockchain This is where the campaign gets more unusual. The attackers are using the BNB Smart Chain test network to store instructions used by the compromised websites. You do not need to understand cryptocurrency to understand why criminals like this setup. Normally, attackers might keep malicious code on a regular web server. Once investigators find that server, a hosting provider may be able to shut it down. A blockchain works differently. In this campaign, the attackers store code inside something called a smart contract. Think of it as a place where the hacked websites can check for their next set of instructions. Netskope says the attackers are using the test version of BNB Smart Chain. Developers normally use this network to experiment without spending real cryptocurrency. That gives the criminals inexpensive infrastructure that can also be harder to take down through traditional methods. There is another advantage. The attacker can change what the smart contract delivers. The compromised websites can then pick up those new instructions without criminals having to modify every hacked site individually. That helps explain why this infrastructure is so useful to them. The campaign is already changing tactics Netskope also found a newer version of the attack that skips the fake CAPTCHA. This version uses technology called WebRTC. Your browser normally uses WebRTC for things such as video calls and real-time communications. The attackers found another use for it. Their code can create an encrypted data connection with the attacker and receive additional malicious code through the browser. Netskope says the code can then run without first being saved as a traditional file on the computer. For you, the technical details are less important than the larger point. The criminals can change how the attack works while continuing to use the same network of compromised websites. 6 ways to protect yourself from fake CAPTCHA malware A few simple habits can help you avoid handing control of your computer to an attacker. 1) Never paste computer commands from a website If a website tells you to open Windows Run, PowerShell or Command Prompt, stop. Do not paste anything it gives you. Close the page instead. 2) Be suspicious of unusual CAPTCHA instructions A normal CAPTCHA may ask you to click a checkbox or identify pictures. It should not require you to change settings or run commands on your PC. Trump told reporters while in Doonbeg, Ireland, that the conflict with Iran will “end after the midterm” elections and that the Iranian regime “wants to make…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday floated the idea that the U.S. could “stay and keep the oil” in Iran, comparing the notion to the U.S.’s major oil deal with Venezuela.

Trump told reporters while in Doonbeg, Ireland, that the conflict with Iran will “end after the midterm” elections and that the Iranian regime “wants to make a deal so badly, and is calling constantly.”

“We’ll ultimately get out unless we decide to stay and keep the oil, like Venezuela,” he later added.

The president previously made similar comments about the conflict ending after the midterms , telling this to reporters at Joint Base Andrews while en route to the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday. Days earlier on Truth Social, Trump said that oil prices driven up by the Iran war “ will drop precipitously ” after the conflict ends.

The Trump administration struck a deal with Venezuela for the U.S. to purchase 20 percent of the oil from North American Blue Energy Partners, a private company that is Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer, at the cost of production.

This oil can then go to fill the U.S.’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which both the Trump and Biden administrations have pulled from in recent years to tackle the rising fuel prices that soared following the start of the Iran war and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

“This 25-year bilateral project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with a production ​target of more than 1.5 million barrels per day,” Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez said on state TV outlet VTV in August. “That ⁠figure relates solely to the bilateral agreement between Venezuela and the United States.”

Trump has sought to control Iran’s oil supply months into the conflict. He told the Financial Times in March that taking the oil was his “favorite thing,” but said that “some stupid people back in the U.S. say: ‘Why are you doing that?’ But they’re stupid people.”

Victoria Coates, vice president of the Institute for National Security and Foreign Policy with the conservative Heritage Foundation, told The Hill at the time that even though the U.S. does not need Iranian oil, it would open the door to businesses entering the country and “rebuilding the industry,” comparing it to Venezuela.

Iran’s shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz greatly bumped up gas prices. The average price of gas in the U.S. hit $4.31 on Sunday, over $1.10 higher than last year’s average, according to data from AAA .

articles.title: Trump Just Promised You $5,000. There’s a Catch, and It Changes Everything About How You’d Spend It.

articles.body:
Trump's "Trump dividend" promises $5,000 to every adult citizen, but lacks a bill, enforcement mechanism, income limits, or delivery timeline.

Tariffs funding the dividend also raise consumer prices, meaning recipients would partly pay themselves back at the register.

If a check arrives, pay off high-interest debt first, given that average credit card APR sits near 21%, then build emergency savings and invest.

Donald Trump told reporters this week that every adult US citizen would receive a $5,000 cash payment if Republicans hold Congress in the midterms, a program he wants branded the "Trump dividend."

In his words, it's $5,000 to every adult. The only caveat is that the dividend must be spent in the United States of America.

The dollar figure gets the headlines. The domestic-spending requirement is what changes how you would actually use it, because a payment you can only spend at US registers behaves very differently from cash in hand.

Our position is straightforward. Treat this as a campaign line rather than a plan, because it is conditional on an election, has no bill attached, and comes with a spending restriction no US cash transfer has ever tried to enforce. You still have work to do now that does not depend on whether the check ever lands.

What Was Promised and What Was Left Blank

Four concrete terms exist: the amount is $5,000, recipients are adult US citizens, Republicans must win the midterms, and the money must be spent inside the country.

Everything else is blank. Trump did not name an income phase-out, a delivery mechanism, a timeline, or a way to police the domestic-spending rule, and he did not point to a legislative vehicle.

He framed the geographic condition bluntly: "We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money. We don't want you going to China, to Germany. You got to spend the money in the United States of America."

articles.title: GOP rep on AI: ‘Let’s get on top of it’
articles.summary: GOP Rep. Mike Flood (Neb.) said Sunday the federal government should implement artificial intelligence safeguards to prevent the technology from falling into the wrong “hands.” During an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Flood said the leaders of top AI companies should be “answering questions” on the safety of the technology and its risks. “This…
articles.body:
GOP Rep. Mike Flood (Neb.) said Sunday the federal government should implement artificial intelligence safeguards to prevent the technology from falling into the wrong “hands.”

During an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Flood said the leaders of top AI companies should be “answering questions” on the safety of the technology and its risks.

“This shouldn’t be ready, shoot, aim or shoot, ready, aim. It should be, ‘Let’s find out what exactly we’re talking about here.’ If it is as dire as they say, obviously, it warrants action, but we need to get the facts before we rush in and say, ‘We’ve got a solution,’” the Nebraska Republican told host Chris Stirewalt.

“I don’t think you could talk to probably 60 percent of the Senate and 60 percent of the House and when somebody says it’s going to lead to world destruction, well, what is that? Tell us exactly what we’re talking about here,” Flood added.

Lawmakers have expressed concern about the risks of rapidly advancing AI models in recent days, after former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon joined multiple AI researchers in sounding alarm bells about the technology.

In announcing his resignation from Anthropic on Tuesday, Coxon said the company and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Coxon wrote on social platform X , “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

In essay he published on Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing the “pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models” to allow risk prevention measures to “keep up.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk concurred with Amodei.

President Trump has generally been receptive to the rapid advancement of AI models as he pushes for the U.S. to win the AI race over China. Trump reiterated his view on Sunday, saying the U.S. is the “most sophisticated country in the world and frankly, I want to keep it that way,”

Trump told reporters in Ireland, “We can put guardrails, and we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen.”

Flood said Sunday he wants the U.S. to build “massive wealth” through AI like it did at the start of the internet age. But he noted he wants “guardrails” on the increasingly ubiquitous technology, noting a country “like Iran could use these tools to manufacture bombs” to use on American cities.

“If we’re at that level and we’re in this unsafe world right now with countries that wake up every day and want to see us destroyed, if they get their hands on this, what does that mean? I mean, this is bigger than shutting down a cellular network,” he told Stirewalt.

“If this is about building something that’s a weapon of mass destruction, let’s get on top of it.”

articles.title: Fund manager's Fed interest rate outlook will frustrate consumers
articles.summary: Here’s what may happen to interest rates at the Federal Reserve’s next open market committee meeting.
articles.body:
Making decisions about how to best spend your hard-earned money isn't easy, particularly nowadays, given how credit card and mortgage rates have risen. Unfortunately, the situation isn't going to get any better anytime soon and may worsen, according to longtime fund manager Chris Versace 's latest Federal Reserve interest rate prediction.

Versace, a money manager who has been tracking markets since the 1990s, believes the next decision from the Fed won't be to cut rates. Instead, he says that the next move is likely an interest rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee meeting wraps up on September 16.

Versace's opinion is that the economic data that has landed over the past few months, including inflation data driven by Middle East oil price pressure, puts Fed Chairman Kevin Warsch in a corner.

The Consumer Price Index data is the final straw for the Fed

We all thought we were making progress in 2024, but the August Consumer Price Index report shows that the Fed's 2% inflation target is nothing more than a pipe dream.

After tariffs caused inflation to stop declining as companies boosted prices and sold less for more (shrinkflation is real), we've now seen the Middle East conflict spike oil prices, which in turn is once again causing prices to climb.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, headline inflation was 3.4% in August . Strip out volatile food and energy costs, and you still see price problems. Core CPI rose 2.4%.

Versace put the Fed's reaction to inflation data bluntly, writing "It's hard to not see the Fed delivering a 25-basis point rate hike," in a note to TheStreet Pro members.

Higher rates are not what the market, consumers, or even the Fed, really want

Stocks have enjoyed a historic AI-frenzy-driven run-up since 2022's bear market drop. Earnings have surged as trillions of dollars have flowed into spinning up controversial data centers nationwide, propping up economic growth.

However, economic growth adds inflationary pressure, and crimping spending by raising the Fed Funds Rate is the Federal Reserve's best way to wrestle inflation lower.

Raising rates to tap down demand, and thus, inflation, works, but is hardly a popular move, especially given how expensive it is to borrow on credit already.

The average credit card interest rate is 19.56%, according to Bankrate . As of September 11, new credit cards charge 23.82%, according to LendingTree .

articles.body:
Democratic Rep. Greg Stanton (Ariz.) said Sunday that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) should keep lawmakers in session to address the risks of rapidly advancing artificial intelligence (AI) models.

“We should take the warnings of the leading investigators of AI very, very seriously,” Stanton told host Chris Stirewalt on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” after a former Anthropic researcher issued a dire warning on Tuesday about the risks of AI .

“Safety and innovation are not the opposite of each other. We can and must do both,” the Arizona Democrat added. “And that’s why we’re demanding Mike Johnson not send Congress home after this week until after the election.”

The House was initially set to be in session the weeks of Sept. 21 and Sept. 28. But House GOP leaders cut the legislative calendar short earlier this month, with lawmakers set to depart Washington, D.C., on Thursday — after a four-day session that follows their 10-day break for Labor Day and Rosh Hashanah.

House lawmakers, like their Senate counterparts , will be out of session for four weeks in October as they campaign ahead of the midterms.

“They should bring us back to Congress, let’s get together and let’s do something on AI safety because the consequences are incredibly serious,” Stanton told Stirewalt, adding that critical infrastructure in the U.S. “could be at risk” if lawmakers do not implement AI safeguards.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) expressed a similar sentiment on Sunday, saying on ABC’s “ This Week ” the lower chamber should “ act urgently ” on AI regulation.

The New York Democrat, though, acknowledged that Republicans “unfortunately” canceled the last two weeks of the lower chamber’s session initially set for later this month.

“We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down … the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely,” Jeffries told host George Stephanopoulos.

Johnson also backed “meaningful regulation” of AI on Sunday, arguing such measures should not “smother American innovation.”

As for keeping lawmakers in town to pass AI regulations, the Louisiana Republican said on NBC’s “ Meet the Press ” he would call a vote on Monday “if we had the solution” to the risks.

“We have to make sure we’re doing it the right way. I think the first step is to have a meeting of all the platform providers,” Johnson told host Kristen Welker, adding he has spoken to President Trump about such a gathering.

articles.title: Centcom commander ‘not concerned at all’ about munitions stockpiles
articles.summary: Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command (Centcom), said he is “not concerned at all” about the U.S.’s munition stockpile amid reports that the Pentagon has depleted its stockpiles to fight Iran. CBS News’s “Face the Nation” aired part of Norah O’Donnell’s interview with Cooper earlier on Sunday, where she asked if the…
articles.body:
Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command (Centcom), said he is “not concerned at all” about the U.S.’s munition stockpile amid reports that the Pentagon has depleted its stockpiles to fight Iran.

CBS News’s “Face the Nation” aired part of Norah O’Donnell’s interview with Cooper earlier on Sunday, where she asked if the munitions depletion during the conflict was a concern.

“I’m not concerned at all,” he replied. “We’re armed and ready for any contingency.”

O’Donnell noted that the U.S. has used 45 percent of its Patriot missiles and more than half of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) missile supply before she asked if this worried him.

President Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. has “ virtually unlimited ” amounts of mid- to high-grade munitions and accused journalists reporting on the depletion of being “treasonous SCUM.”

“In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen,” he wrote on Truth Social, adding that weapons sales to allies will resume “soon again.”

The U.S. and Iran have exchanged on-and-off strikes on each other as the conflict stretched into its seventh month. The conflict has put a strain on the Pentagon’s stockpiles of various long-range missiles, with the U.S. having an estimated 759 and 827 Patriot missile interceptors, down from 2,330 the day before in July, according to analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)

The THAAD interceptor stockpile was also down from 452 before the conflict to between 234 and 278 on July 27, the CSIS also noted.

If Trump deployed an expanded airstrike campaign in Iran, the drop in munition quantity could force the U.S. military to lean more on piloted bombing missions .

The Pentagon also reached a deal last month with Northrop Grumman to increase production of THAAD and Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptors. But industry experts have told The Hill and other news outlets that it will take a few years at minimum for the U.S. to rebuild its stockpile to pre-Iran war levels.

The conflict has seen both countries exchange fire in recent weeks, with Iranian media reporting Sunday that a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an “ unidentified projectile ,” killing one crew member and injuring four more. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations organization also reported a vessel being struck in the strait.

Trump said he would not say whether U.S. forces were behind the attack. The Hill has reached out to Centcom for comment.

articles.title: Pennsylvania woman dies from measles complications
articles.summary: The Jefferson County, Pa., Coroner’s Office on Sunday said a 40-year-old woman died from complications with measles, the state’s third measles-related death this year. Coroner Greg Furlong wrote on Facebook that the woman, a Jefferson County resident, died on Saturday. He added that his office was working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on this…
articles.body:
The Jefferson County, Pa., Coroner’s Office on Sunday said a 40-year-old woman died from complications with measles, the state’s third measles-related death this year.

Coroner Greg Furlong wrote on Facebook that the woman, a Jefferson County resident, died on Saturday. He added that his office was working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on this case.

“This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease,” Furlong wrote. “Our thoughts and prayers are with the family during this difficult time. We ask that the public and media respect their privacy as they mourn the loss of their loved one.”

The Hill has reached out to the Pennsylvania Department of Health for comment.

The department told NBC News that it was aware of the woman’s death and that it was “conducting a thorough review of this case and will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available.”

Jefferson County Chief Deputy Coroner and public relations officer Jason Stiver emphasized that the public remain aware of the disease and follow guidance from health officials.

“While cases of severe illness remain uncommon, this tragedy highlights that measles should not be taken lightly,” Stiver said in Furlong’s statement. “Public health measures, early recognition of symptoms, and consultation with healthcare providers are important tools in protecting our community.”

Measles symptoms typically begin 7-14 days after infection, beginning with fever, a cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, along with a red rash, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) .

The disease is dangerous to babies and young children and can cause severe complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain.

Pennsylvania health officials earlier this month reported the “measles-related” deaths of two unvaccinated people in Lancaster County, including an infant, as the state grapples with an outbreak that has sickened 676 people and hospitalized 124 as of Friday, department officials stated . The two deaths marked the first measles-related deaths in the state in 35 years and the first in the U.S. this year.

The CDC disputed the two deaths and excluded them from its official weekly tally of deaths. The deaths were not included on the CDC’s website. An asterisk on the agency’s website stated that they will not be included “while CDC reviews additional information regarding the circumstances and causes of death.”

“At this time, available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles,” the message stated. “CDC will update the national count as additional information becomes available.”

CDC Director Erica Schwartz has made no public appearances or remarks amid the outbreak. Any information coming out of the agency has been from social media and overtly political.

articles.title: Air Force colonel recounts how he survived after F-15E jet was shot down over Iran
articles.summary: A U.S. Air Force colonel recounted his story of survival after his F-15E fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April, in the early months of the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran. The colonel spoke with “60 Minutes” on CBS News about the incident and was referred to by the outlet as Bravo, his mission…
articles.body:
A U.S. Air Force colonel recounted his story of survival after his F-15E fighter jet was shot down over Iran in April, in the early months of the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran.

The colonel spoke with “60 Minutes” on CBS News about the incident and was referred to by the outlet as Bravo, his mission call sign, due to security threats. Bravo told Norah O’Donnell that he was the weapon-systems officer of the two-man crew when their plane was struck and he plummeted at an estimated 70-100 mph.

“At one point when I looked up and saw no parachute, that was the most terrifying thing I’ve ever seen,” Bravo said, with his parachute damaged by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile. “So I paused, right then, and I prayed, ‘Lord, your will be done. But if I’m getting through this, I need help.'”

The crew’s mission, named with the mission call sign Dude 44, was to conduct a strike on Iranian industrial facilities tied to the country’s drone and missile program, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) commander Adm. Brad Cooper told O’Donnell.

Bravo compared the missile striking the jet to “getting hit by a freight train.” Bravo and his partner, with the mission call sign Alpha, ejected when they could not save the jet. Alpha ejected safely, but Bravo landed hard about 5 miles away. Both ended up in Isfahan, Iran.

“I had injuries, but we all train to adapt and overcome the things that we’re faced with,” he said. “I moved as quickly as I could, despite the injuries, away from the place that I landed.”

Bravo broke his back, an arm and a shoulder after he hit the ground, but he managed to hike up to a 7,000-foot ridgeline. He described his survival as a “modern-day miracle.” Bravo found himself in a valley with cliffs on either side. Iranian forces reached within a few hundred meters of Bravo’s location, CBS News reported, citing military sources.

A U.S. rescue team found Alpha six hours after the jet was shot down. Bravo said he was able to alert U.S. forces that he was hurt but still moving. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told O’Donnell that it was a “really tough decision” after learning of Bravo’s whereabouts and after the rescue team’s helicopter took fire from Iranian forces. Hegseth determined that Bravo would be rescued in another 24 hours.

Another day passed with almost no water or food in the harsh environment before two rescue planes located him. Sand became stuck in the planes’ landing gear, leaving more than 90 of what Cooper called the military’s “most elite service members” stuck on Iranian soil.

The service members destroyed the planes before more U.S. forces picked them up, to prevent them from falling into Iranian hands.

“It’s a story of the teamwork, the training, of the faith, of the decisions and the leadership to do something that will live in history as an example of what America’s willing to do, in order to uphold our promise and leave no man behind,” Bravo told O’Donnell.

The Iran war has stretched into its seventh month, with the U.S. and Iran exchanging fire in recent weeks. President Trump has said the conflict will end after the midterm elections and suggested that the U.S. could take control of Iran’s oil supply , similar to the U.S. oil deal with Venezuela, as the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz has left gas prices soaring since March.

articles.title: White House agrees to new ethics language in crypto bill
articles.summary: The White House has agreed to new ethics language in the Clarity Act ahead of a key vote on the cryptocurrency regulation bill in the Senate on Tuesday. The provision, which bars public officials from issuing or sponsoring digital assets, could be enforced by both state attorneys general and the Department of Justice (DOJ) under…
articles.body:
The White House has agreed to new ethics language in the Clarity Act ahead of a key vote on the cryptocurrency regulation bill in the Senate on Tuesday.

The provision, which bars public officials from issuing or sponsoring digital assets, could be enforced by both state attorneys general and the Department of Justice (DOJ) under updated language released by Senate Republicans late Sunday.

This was a key demand from Democrats, whose support is needed to clear Tuesday’s procedural vote on the Senate floor.

“After a year of intense daily bipartisan negotiations, this bill is ready,” Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) said in a statement.

It’s unclear whether the updated ethics provision will be enough to win over key Democrats. A Senate GOP aide said Sunday that Trump agreed to about 80 percent of what was requested.

Democrats have long sought an ethics provision in the Clarity Act in the face of concerns about President Trump and his family’s involvement in the crypto industry .

The White House agreed to ethics language in late July, but Democrats pushed back on the decision to put the DOJ in charge of enforcement.

“A no vote on Tuesday means opposing real ethics reforms on politicians’ personal investments, handing American leadership in digital assets to our foreign competitors, and leaving Americans with zero protections in the digital asset markets,” Lummis added. “Democrats got what they wanted; now they need to take yes for an answer.”
