articles.summary: By Rashika Singh Sept 14 (Reuters) - Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan now expect the U.S.
articles.body:
Sept 14 (Reuters) - Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan now expect the U.S. Federal Reserve to raise interest rates this week after a string of ‌stronger-than-expected inflation readings challenged hopes that price pressures would continue to ease without ‌additional policy tightening.

The Wall Street banks joined a growing number of forecasters turning more hawkish after data last ​week showed U.S. consumer and producer prices rose more than expected in August, while oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel due to renewed hostilities in the Middle East. [O/R]

In a note on Friday, Goldman Sachs abandoned its previous call for rates to remain unchanged and now expects a ‌25-basis-point increase at the U.S. Fed's ⁠September 15-16 meeting. J.P. Morgan, meanwhile, forecasts quarter-point hikes in both September and December.

The latest data have revived concerns that progress toward the ⁠Fed's 2% inflation target could stall after months of moderation.

"We think that the FOMC will be reluctant to surprise," Goldman Sachs economist David Mericle said.

J.P. Morgan struck a similarly hawkish tone following the ​inflation ​reports.

"The week that saw rising bond yields and ​energy prices and a firm enough ‌set of inflation readings to make a rate hike at next week's FOMC meeting more likely than not," J.P. Morgan economists led by Michael Feroli said in a note.

The outlook for further Fed tightening will be in focus this week as policymakers conclude their meeting on Wednesday, while investors also watch the Bank of Japan for policy signals.

J.P. Morgan said the ‌latest inflation data cast doubt on a sustained ​disinflation trend, leading it to forecast another Fed rate ​hike this year and raise its estimate ​of the long-run policy rate to 3.25%.

Markets are pricing in an ‌87% chance of a quarter-point Fed rate ​hike this month, up ​from about 70% before the latest inflation data, with another increase expected in December, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.

In a separate note on Sunday, Goldman Sachs said it ​still expects two Fed rate ‌cuts in 2027, though later than previously forecast, as it sees this week's ​expected hike as driven more by market pricing than inflation fundamentals.

(Reporting by ​Rashika Singh in Bengaluru; Editing by Sherry Jacob-Phillips)

articles.body:
Markets overwhelmingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates this week for the first time in more than three years — but the decision is likely to be a closer call than investors' bets suggest.

"The probabilities in the market seem higher than I would necessarily assign at this point," Loretta Mester, former president of the Cleveland Fed, said in an interview. Mester pointed to recent arguments by key members of the Fed's rate-setting committee, New York Fed president John Williams and Fed Governor Chris Waller, suggesting that neither is convinced a rate hike is appropriate.

However, key inflation data released Friday boosted market expectations for a hike. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) for August showed monthly prices rose 0.3%, higher than the expected 0.2%, crossing a symbolic line in the sand drawn by a handful of Fed officials. Since Friday, traders have been pricing in between 85% and 90% odds that the Fed will raise 25 basis points.

Waller has said that if August figures showed cooling inflation — specifically a 0.2% rise in core prices — he would support holding rates steady. But if inflation came in "hot," he would consider a hike. "Policy is currently only slightly restricting aggregate demand," Waller said on Sept. 3, "and it may not take much acceleration in inflation to nudge me into supporting tighter policy."

Meanwhile, Williams has argued that monthly Personal Consumption Expenditures readings — the Fed's preferred yardstick — must consistently hit 0.2% to prove inflation is truly coming down.

While the latest CPI data has made Adam Posen, president of the Peterson Institute for International Economics, less certain of a pause, he still thinks the central bank is more likely than not to hold rates steady.

"Ideally, the Fed should never be making up their minds based on one last-minute piece of data," Posen said. "This is why when you say 'I don't want to do forecasts,' it's self-defeating. Otherwise, you're just reacting to a backward-looking, inherently noisy reading."

Last month in Jackson Hole, Wyo., Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh laid out a cogent case for raising rates . He noted that June and July inflation reports failed to prove prices are on a convincing downward path , adding that he would be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as "restrictive."

Yet, Posen maintains that a hike right now would require multiple board members to abruptly reverse their recent dovish stances. Doing so would also mean taking responsibility for "putting the Fed directly back in the crosshairs of Trump's political ire."

articles.title: Compound in blueberries may help muscles burn fat, study finds
articles.summary: A natural compound found in blueberries and grapes helped muscle cells burn stored fat in lab tests, researchers found.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A natural compound found in blueberries, grapes and other berries could help muscles burn excess fat instead of storing it

Researchers in Japan identified the compound, called pterostilbene, and found that it reduced fat buildup by increasing the breakdown of stored fat in laboratory tests using mouse muscle cells.

Pterostilbene works by protecting PPARδ, or PPAR-delta, a protein that helps cells burn fatty acids for energy. By preventing PPARδ from breaking down, the compound boosts the activity of genes involved in converting fat into energy.

“Our findings establish a scientific framework for developing functional foods and nutritional supplements that target muscle fat metabolism,” Associate Professor Takakazu Mitani said in a release from Shinshu University .

Researchers said the findings could help guide the development of foods, supplements and treatments aimed at reducing fat accumulation in muscle tissue.

Excess fat inside muscle cells can interfere with how the body processes glucose and fatty acids, a problem linked to obesity, insulin resistance , Type 2 diabetes and aging.

So far, the research has only been conducted on lab-grown mouse muscle cells.

Scientists have not yet studied the effects in humans or other animals with more complex metabolisms, so it remains unclear whether the compound will produce similar results outside the laboratory.

The findings were published earlier this month in the journal Food Bioscience .

articles.title: What happens after a town de-Flocks
articles.summary: Cities across the US are ditching the controversial license plate-reading cameras, but some are now turning to new surveillance tools.﻿
articles.body: From Florida to Washington state, local governments across the country are canceling their contracts with Flock, the company behind the controversial AI-enabled license plate readers, in response to public outcry. But ending the contracts doesn’t necessarily mean the cameras will come down immediately — or that the information they’ve gathered will be deleted anytime soon. Even as state and local governments decide to rein in their surveillance capabilities, uncertainty remains about what Flock can and will do with data that has already been collected. Each jurisdiction’s contract is different, but many of them let Flock retain data long after it’s been collected. “Let’s say they terminate,” said Saira Hussain, a senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation who has reviewed dozens of municipal Flock contracts. “What happens to the data, and how long is it able to be searched? That question appears to be unresolved.” The backlash against Flock was slow to mount, but now it’s everywhere, and it’s bipartisan. Founded in 2017, Flock pitched its cameras — which are sold not only to local governments but to private businesses and citizens — as an unobtrusive tool to enhance public safety. Early in the company’s history, some cities even offered grants for homeowners associations that wanted to install Flock cameras in their neighborhoods. Flock’s footprint has grown quickly. The company has installed more than 120,000 cameras across the US. This rapid expansion, along with alarming reports of misuses of Flock’s surveillance network, has fueled a new wave of opposition, making Flock a kind of shorthand for privacy invasion. In recent months, activists in big cities and small towns have urged local governments to end their contracts, citing concerns about privacy, harassment, and mass surveillance. Local leaders have said the public pressure — coupled with Flock’s data-sharing and retention policies, and what the company can do with the information its cameras collect — spurred them to end the contracts. Lawmakers in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, unanimously voted to end the city’s Flock contract after learning that Flock reportedly tried to sell anonymized data collected in Sheboygan back to the city’s public works department. Elsewhere in the state, the mayor of Stevens Point not only ended its contract with Flock but also covered up the 10 cameras scattered throughout the city. “We really have no way of auditing where the Flock data goes once it’s collected,” Mayor Mike Wiza said on a local radio show. “Our community is not comfortable using these cameras without some assurances that it’s being used in a manner we have authorized.” (Flock maintains that it doesn’t sell consumer data.) Local leaders across the country say they were misled about how Flock data could be used, and some have admitted that they didn’t realize the degree to which the data would be accessed by third parties. In Bridgewater, Virginia, the town council put bags over its Flock cameras after voting to cancel its contract. Bridgewater is home to fewer than 7,000 people, but the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism found that because of the town’s information-sharing agreement with Flock, data collected in the town was searched 7 million times by law enforcement in 12 months. The EFF, which sued the city of San Jose, California, over its usage of Flock cameras, argues that these information-sharing agreements violate the Fourth Amendment’s protections against unreasonable search and seizure. “Through these searches, police are able to identify patterns of where people live and work, where they may drop off their kids to school, who they associate with, where they worship, seek reproductive care, seek an immigration consult,” Hussain said. “What we’re talking about here is a mass surveillance technology that is by design intended to identify where people are going and track people’s movements.” Like many movements against law enforcement overreach, the backlash against Flock began with stories about particularly egregious abuses. There have been several reports of law enforcement officers using Flock to track exes and romantic partners. In response to these and other concerns, Flock recently rolled out new guardrails, including a new requirement to run case codes — which were previously optional — for all searches. Flock is also mandating a feature called Audit Assistance, which flags “abnormal” queries. “This is such an obvious way to curb abuse,” Flock CEO Garrett Langley recently told The Verge. “And I said, ‘Fine. You know what? I think that’s right, and we got this one wrong. We should make it a requirement.’” Flock has also shortened its standard data retention period from 30 to seven days, though it will let individual jurisdictions lengthen these time frames. Agencies that use Flock will also be able to limit what kinds of information they share with other entities. For example, a city or police department could let other jurisdictions access its Flock data for homicide searches, but not for queries related to immigration enforcement. But privacy advocates say Flock’s reforms don’t go far enough. The American Civil Liberties Union, which is suing San Jose alongside the EFF, said the changes are “more focused on addressing a perceived PR problem than the significant harms its products create.” It’s unclear what would stop someone from falsely or incorrectly tagging a Flock search. For example, after sheriff’s deputies in one Texas county used Flock to track a woman suspected of violating the state’s abortion ban, the sheriff described the queries as a search for a missing person. Flock has repeatedly emphasized that Immigration and Customs Enforcement doesn’t have access to its cameras. But local agencies that have deputized their officers under federal 287(g) agreements — which let local law enforcement conduct immigration arrests — can use Flock for immigration enforcement, and many do. Public recordsobtained by 404 Media revealed that Florida’s Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission uses Flock to carry out ICE arrests. The agency is reportedly also using Flock to surveil and track its critics. Florida’s Department of Transportation has since banned Flock cameras from state highways, but law enforcement can still tap into city- and county-level Flock cameras, or to those installed on private property. Shopping centers, retail giants like Home Depot and Lowe’s, and homeowners associations have reportedly installed Flock cameras on their properties. Activists are urging beauty retailer Ulta to drop its Flock contracts, citing numerous reports of officers using the surveillance network to track women. Privacy activists note that ending Flock contracts won’t be enough to stop mass surveillance. Some cities that have ended their relationships with Flock — including South Pasadena, California, and Durango, Colorado — are now considering alternatives. The Flock backlash has reportedly enriched Axon, the company that also makes Tasers and body-worn cameras. Hussain notes that Axon’s system is arguably more integrated than Flock’s. “Axon has other technologies as well that they stack on top of their automated license plate readers. They have a bunch of other data streams, including coming from their body-worn cameras, so you’re able to build out quite a surveillance system,” she said. “You’re not going to be able to stop this mass surveillance technology by moving to another vendor. The only thing that is going to solve this whole problem is not relying on this technology.”

articles.title: Trump: ‘I’m not downplaying’ AI risks
articles.summary: President Trump pushed back on reports he is “downplaying” artificial intelligence (AI) risks after industry leaders over the weekend pressed for slowing down the development of the technology. “This week, again, there’s been so much concern about AI. Have you heard directly from any of these AI tech leaders? And you seemed to downplay some…
articles.body:
President Trump pushed back on reports he is “downplaying” artificial intelligence (AI) risks after industry leaders over the weekend pressed for slowing down the development of the technology.

“This week, again, there’s been so much concern about AI. Have you heard directly from any of these AI tech leaders? And you seemed to downplay some of the concerns that we’ve heard —” a reporter asked the president Sunday aboard Air Force One .

“No, I’m not downplaying,” Trump cut in. “But it’s going to be more good than bad, by a lot.”

Earlier in the day, while the president was at a golf tournament in Ireland, Trump was asked about slowing down AI development or increasing regulation of the industry.

“Well, I’ll say this: we’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” the president said.

“And we can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but, I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” he added.

On Saturday. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued AI development needed to slow down to give space for the implementation of necessary risk prevention safeguards, with fellow tech moguls OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and billionaire Elon Musk backing him up.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

The Anthropic CEO recommended that AI companies quickly undertake measures aimed at “pacing” the development of models and warned of potentially grim consequences if the technology does not have brakes.

“To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models, and for third party evaluators to confirm this,” he continued. “Our pacing framework is an attempt to further strengthen our commitment to safety and encourage a race to the top.”

The conversation also comes as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle push for more briefings and safeguards around the emerging technology. Though some, like House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), have urged others not to panic.

Earlier this month, a study from a group of current and former Anthropic researchers offered a stark warning , suggesting the AI they are working on could destroy humanity .
